meta.name: Microsoft Azure Virtual Desktop Specialty (AZ-140)
meta.notes: Initial pack — covers host pool design, FSLogix profiles, MSIX app attach, autoscale, conditional access, monitoring, and image management. [hardening pass (scheduled-agent 2026-08-10): re-shuffled 11/12 correct positions to 3/3/3/3 with no adjacent repeats, fixed length tells on Q002/Q004/Q005/Q007/Q010/Q011 so no correct answer is uniquely longest, tightened distractors to parallel phrasing across all 12 questions, rewrote every explanation to explicitly refute each distractor by name, stripped stem-word echoes from correct options on Q001/Q004/Q010]

questions.question: A team plans an Azure Virtual Desktop deployment for 200 task workers who all need the same shared Windows 11 multi-session desktop with identical apps and policies. Users routinely sign in to whichever VM has the most free capacity. Which host pool type should you choose?
options: Personal host pool with automatic assignment, so each user keeps a dedicated VM across sessions
Personal host pool with direct assignment, pre-binding every user to a named session host in advance
Pooled host pool with depth-first load balancing, packing sessions onto one host before opening the next
Pooled host pool with breadth-first load balancing, spreading each new session across the hosts
questions.explanation: Pooled host pools let many users share the same session hosts (typically Windows 11 multi-session) and are the fit for identical, interchangeable task-worker desktops. Breadth-first load balancing sends each new session to the least-used host, keeping capacity spread evenly — exactly the behaviour the scenario describes. Depth-first packs one host until a session-limit threshold is hit and is normally paired with a scaling plan that stops idle hosts for cost savings, not for balanced steady-state load. Personal host pools with automatic or direct assignment dedicate one VM per user, so 200 users would need 200 always-on VMs and no sharing — the opposite of the requirement.

questions.question: Users on a pooled Windows 11 multi-session host pool complain that their Outlook signatures, OneDrive sync state, and Teams cache are lost every time they land on a different session host. You need a Microsoft-supported profile solution that roams the full user profile and is entitled by the AVD license. What should you deploy?
options: FSLogix profile containers stored on Azure Files or Azure NetApp Files, mounted at logon
Roaming user profiles synchronised through Active Directory Group Policy on each host
Mandatory profiles baked into the gold image and copied to each host's local C: drive
Windows User State Virtualization with folder redirection to a highly available file share
questions.explanation: FSLogix profile containers are the Microsoft-recommended profile solution for AVD and are entitled by the AVD license. Each user profile is stored as a VHD/VHDX on Azure Files (with Entra Kerberos or AD DS Kerberos) or Azure NetApp Files, and is dynamically mounted on whichever session host the user lands on — preserving Outlook OST, OneDrive cache, Teams data and app settings. Roaming user profiles copy a shrunken profile subset at logon/logoff and do not reliably handle large OST files or modern per-user AppData. Mandatory profiles are read-only, so signature and cache changes are discarded at sign-out by design. Folder redirection alone leaves modern-app state (Teams, OneDrive, Outlook OST) behind because those live under AppData\Local, not in the redirected shell folders.

questions.question: You are sizing an Azure Files Premium share to host FSLogix profile containers for 500 AVD users. Microsoft publishes a per-user steady-state IOPS target for this workload. Approximately what minimum IOPS should the share sustain to meet that baseline recommendation?
options: About 5 IOPS per user — provision roughly 2,500 IOPS for the 500-user share
About 200 IOPS per user — provision roughly 100,000 IOPS for the 500-user share
About 10 IOPS per user — provision roughly 5,000 IOPS for the 500-user share
About 50 IOPS per user — provision roughly 25,000 IOPS for the 500-user share
questions.explanation: Microsoft's published FSLogix sizing guidance is roughly 10 IOPS per user at steady state, so 500 users → ~5,000 IOPS as a baseline; bursts to 50+ IOPS per user occur during logon/logoff storms and need extra headroom. The 5-IOPS figure is undersized and will queue I/O even at steady state, causing profile mount stalls. The 50-IOPS figure is the burst target, not the steady-state baseline — provisioning to it permanently wastes premium capacity. The 200-IOPS estimate is roughly 20× the documented steady-state number and would over-provision the share dramatically. Remember that Premium file shares scale IOPS with provisioned size (about 1 IOPS per GiB + a baseline), so size for whichever of IOPS or capacity is larger.

questions.question: Your security team requires multi-factor authentication on every Azure Virtual Desktop connection, including reconnects, with no MFA prompts skipped due to remember-device tokens. Which single configuration meets the requirement?
options: Enable Entra ID security defaults — they force MFA on every AVD reconnect regardless of remember-me tokens
A Conditional Access policy on the Azure Virtual Desktop app requiring MFA, with sign-in frequency Every time
Enable legacy per-user MFA on every user account, which overrides any Conditional Access sign-in-frequency window
An Entra ID Protection user-risk policy set to High — remediation forces MFA on every subsequent sign-in
questions.explanation: The supported way to force MFA on every reconnect is a Conditional Access policy targeting the Azure Virtual Desktop cloud app (and, for Entra-joined hosts, the Windows Cloud Login app) with 'Require MFA' as a grant control and Sign-in frequency set to 'Every time' — this defeats token caching and reprompts on every session, exactly what the security team wants. Security defaults enforce MFA on new sign-ins but keep default remember-device windows, so reconnects can skip the prompt. Legacy per-user MFA is enforced by the older service and does not override Conditional Access — Microsoft is deprecating it and recommends CA instead. User-risk policies fire only when Identity Protection judges the user risky, not on every session, so they do not deterministically enforce MFA on each reconnect.

questions.question: You publish only Microsoft Edge and a finance line-of-business application from a pooled host pool, exposing them as RemoteApp programs rather than a full desktop. Which AVD object type must the app group be?
options: Desktop application group — the auto-created desktop group also holds published RemoteApp programs
Workspace object — RemoteApp programs are registered directly under the workspace with no app group
Host pool object — RemoteApp publishing is configured on the host pool, not on an application group
A separate RemoteApp application group linked to the host pool, distinct from the desktop group
questions.explanation: Each AVD host pool comes with one auto-created Desktop application group that publishes the full desktop, and it can also have one or more RemoteApp application groups where you publish individual programs — Edge and the finance app here. You then assign users or groups to that RemoteApp group. Adding RemoteApp programs to the Desktop application group is not how it works; that group only publishes the full desktop. Workspaces aggregate app groups so end users see them in Feed Discovery, but they do not host applications directly. Host pools carry session hosts and settings, not the app-publishing metadata — that lives on the application group.

questions.question: You need to deliver a Win32 application to AVD session hosts without baking it into the gold image and without installing it locally on each VM, so that updates can be rolled out by replacing a single package. Which AVD feature fits?
options: FSLogix Office Container — designed to stream Win32 desktop apps to sessions on demand
Azure App Service deployment slots — swap app versions without redeploying the session hosts
MSIX app attach — attach a single MSIX package as a VHD/CIM to user sessions at logon
Windows Update for Business with Autopatch — deliver the app installer via Intune to every host
questions.explanation: MSIX app attach stages a single MSIX package (VHD, VHDX or CIM) on a file share, registers it with the host pool, and dynamically attaches it to user sessions at logon — updating the package on the share replaces the app for every session with no per-host reinstall, matching the requirement exactly. FSLogix Office Container is a profile-adjacent container for Outlook OST and OneDrive data; it is not an application-delivery mechanism and does not stream Win32 apps. Azure App Service is a PaaS web-hosting platform and does not run apps on session hosts at all. Autopatch and Intune push installs to each machine, which is exactly the per-host reinstall pattern the question rules out.

questions.question: After business hours your pooled host pool sits mostly idle, but you still pay full VM compute. You want Azure to automatically start hosts in the morning, stop them after hours, and use depth-first load balancing during ramp-down to drain hosts before stopping. Which native AVD feature should you configure?
options: An AVD scaling plan on the host pool with ramp-up, peak, ramp-down and off-peak schedules
Azure Automation runbook running Start-AzVM and Stop-AzVM on a PowerShell time-trigger
VM auto-shutdown, configured in each session host's VM blade to stop them at a fixed clock time
Azure Monitor autoscale rules attached to a VM Scale Set hosting the session VMs
questions.explanation: An AVD scaling plan is the first-party feature for time-based start/stop of session hosts on both pooled and personal host pools. You define daily schedules (ramp-up, peak, ramp-down, off-peak), and each phase can specify its own load-balancing algorithm — during ramp-down AVD switches to depth-first so users drain onto fewer hosts, letting the rest deallocate for cost savings, which is exactly the scenario. Automation runbooks with Start-AzVM/Stop-AzVM work mechanically but ignore user sessions and AVD load balancing, and Microsoft explicitly steers customers to scaling plans instead. VM auto-shutdown in the VM blade stops hosts on a clock without draining active sessions, disconnecting users mid-work. AVD session hosts are provisioned as regular VMs, not as a Virtual Machine Scale Set, so Azure Monitor VMSS autoscale rules don't apply to a host pool.

questions.question: You are deploying Windows 11 multi-session session hosts that must be joined directly to Microsoft Entra ID (no AD DS, no Entra Domain Services). Users authenticate with Entra ID accounts and FSLogix profiles are stored on Azure Files. Which storage authentication option must the file share use?
options: On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) Kerberos on a domain-joined storage account
Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid identities on the storage account, no domain join required
Microsoft Entra Domain Services (Entra DS) Kerberos on the storage account, backed by a managed domain
Shared storage-account key access — Kerberos is not required when the hosts are Entra-joined
questions.explanation: For Entra-joined session hosts using Azure Files to store FSLogix profiles, the supported and recommended option is Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid identities — the storage account is not domain-joined, users get NTFS/ACL permissions via their hybrid identity, and Kerberos tickets are issued by Entra ID directly. AD DS Kerberos requires the storage account to be joined to an on-prem AD DS domain and works only when the session hosts are AD DS or hybrid-joined, which contradicts the scenario. Entra DS Kerberos requires a Microsoft Entra Domain Services managed domain, an extra billable service the scenario explicitly rules out. Storage-account-key access is not supported by FSLogix (no per-user ACL enforcement) and Microsoft explicitly advises against it.

questions.question: You want a session host image that is patched monthly, has the AVD agent installed, FSLogix configured, Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise with shared computer activation enabled, and is versioned for staged rollout across regions. Which Azure service combination provides the recommended pipeline?
options: Sysprep a single VM manually, upload the VHD, and register it as a managed image for host-pool deployment
Azure Backup recovery points of a template VM, used as the base for new session-host deployments
Azure DevTest Labs custom images attached directly to the host-pool deployment template
Azure Image Builder writing versioned images into an Azure Compute Gallery image definition
questions.explanation: The recommended modern pipeline is Azure VM Image Builder (a managed Packer service) that runs the monthly patching, agent install, FSLogix and M365 Apps steps and publishes the output as versioned images inside an Azure Compute Gallery image definition. The Gallery handles cross-region replication, version retention and staged rollout, and it is directly consumable by host-pool deployment ARM/Bicep templates and by scaling operations. Manual sysprep + managed image works but is not repeatable, has no versioning story, and Microsoft's guidance explicitly recommends Image Builder + Compute Gallery instead. Azure Backup produces recovery points for disaster recovery of running VMs — they are not distributable images and cannot be replicated across regions as image versions. DevTest Labs is a lab-oriented service (auto-shutdown of dev VMs, quotas) whose custom images are scoped to the lab, not intended for production host-pool deployments.

questions.question: Support needs to investigate why a specific user takes 90+ seconds to sign in to AVD. You want to break down logon time by stages — connection, group policy, FSLogix profile load, user profile, shell load — using a Microsoft-provided workbook. Where should you look?
options: Azure Service Health blade filtered to the Azure Virtual Desktop service, looking at incident timelines
Microsoft Defender for Cloud secure-score recommendations for the host pool's session hosts
The Azure Virtual Desktop Insights workbook in Azure Monitor, in its Connection Diagnostics section
Network Watcher Connection Monitor configured between the client subnet and the session hosts
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual Desktop Insights is a curated Azure Monitor workbook (per host pool and per session host) that ingests AVD diagnostic-setting data and session-host agent telemetry. Its Connection Diagnostics section breaks the logon into stages — connection, group policy, FSLogix profile load, user-profile load, shell load — which is exactly what a per-user slow-logon investigation needs. Azure Service Health only surfaces platform-level incidents against the AVD service and shows nothing per-user or per-stage. Defender for Cloud reports security posture and hardening recommendations, not per-user connection timings. Network Watcher Connection Monitor measures reachability and latency between endpoints but has no visibility into FSLogix, GPO or shell-load stages that happen after the network hop.

questions.question: A finance group must connect to AVD only from corporate-managed Windows devices and only from the corporate public IP ranges. They must still get the standard MFA prompt on connection. Which Conditional Access configuration meets all three requirements?
options: Grant requiring MFA and requiring a compliant device, with a Locations condition for the corporate named IP location
Grant access that only requires MFA — the AVD client itself checks Intune device compliance, so a CA control isn't needed
A sign-in-risk policy set to Medium, letting Entra ID Protection evaluate device and location signals together
Block all locations except a trusted-IP named location, and exclude the finance group from MFA so connections stay quick
questions.explanation: A Conditional Access policy on the Azure Virtual Desktop cloud app (and the Windows Cloud Login app for Entra-joined hosts) should combine three controls: Require MFA and Require compliant device as grant controls, plus a Locations condition restricted to the corporate named IP location — all three requirements land in one policy. The 'MFA only' option relies on the AVD client to enforce compliance, but the AVD client does not check compliance itself; that must be a Conditional Access grant control. A sign-in-risk policy fires remediation only when Identity Protection judges the sign-in risky, so a Medium risk policy does not deterministically enforce device compliance or a location on every session. The last option directly violates the 'standard MFA prompt' requirement by excluding finance users from MFA.

questions.question: You are deploying a personal host pool for 50 developers, each needing a persistent VM. You want a new joiner to be auto-assigned to the first available host in the pool at first sign-in, with no admin intervention. Which assignment type should the host pool use?
options: Direct assignment — an admin must pre-map every user to a specific host before their first sign-in
Automatic assignment — on first sign-in the user is bound to the next available host permanently
Pooled assignment — the user is load-balanced across hosts on every session, as in a shared desktop
Group assignment — every member of a security group shares one host on a first-come basis
questions.explanation: Personal host pools support exactly two assignment types. Automatic assignment binds the user to the first available host at first sign-in and persists that mapping — no admin intervention needed for new joiners, matching the scenario. Direct assignment requires an admin to pre-map each user to a specific host before they can connect, which is exactly what the question rules out. 'Pooled assignment' is not a personal-host-pool assignment type at all — pooled is the other host-pool type (shared desktops with load balancing). 'Group assignment' is not a real AVD assignment type either; there is no group-based sharing model on a personal host pool because the host-to-user mapping is 1:1.
